name: Sleeping on your back

lead: Some looksmaxxers sleep on their backs so the face stays off the pillow, aiming to avoid sleep lines, the creases that form when the face is pressed into a pillow or mattress for hours.

The idea is that avoiding repeated overnight compression of facial skin reduces creasing over time. Wikipedia's article on wrinkles states that habitual sleeping positions are linked to wrinkles, citing a dermatology-society resource, but gives no study detail. No published trial has tested whether changing sleep position alters facial wrinkles.

paras: People train themselves to sleep face-up, often using a supportive pillow arrangement so they stay on their back. Lateral (side) sleeping is the most common adult position, followed by supine, then prone.
Sleep research links supine sleep to worse positional sleep apnea, reflux after meals and more sleep paralysis in some people. It is not discussed as a cosmetic risk.

angle.text: Some looksmaxxing practitioners sleep face-up to avoid sleep lines caused by pressing the face into a pillow for hours. With the face off the pillow there is no overnight compression, so fewer creases form. Habitual sleep position is linked to wrinkles in reference sources, and no trial has tested changing position.

lead: Sleeping on your back (the supine position) is a sleep posture that some looksmaxxing practitioners adopt in the belief that it avoids so-called sleep lines, the facial creases attributed to pressing the face into a pillow or mattress for hours each night.[1][2]

Reference sources describe three main sleep positions in adults: lateral (on the side), supine (face up) and prone (face down). The lateral position is the most common, followed by supine and then prone.[1] Wikipedia's article on wrinkles states that habitual sleeping positions are linked to wrinkles, citing a dermatology-society resource, but gives no study detail for the claim.[2] No published trial has been located that tests whether changing sleep position alters facial wrinkles.
infobox: Avoid sleep lines and facial creasing

paras: The practice consists of lying face up for sleep rather than on the side or stomach, so that the cheeks, forehead and chin are not compressed against a pillow. Some adherents combine it with other habits, such as pillow choice, but those details vary between individuals.

Sleep-medicine literature summarised on Wikipedia notes that the supine position is associated with several health-related effects unrelated to appearance. Positional obstructive sleep apnea is reported to account for roughly 56 to 75 percent of regular obstructive sleep apnea cases, and avoiding supine sleep is the basis of positional therapy.[1] Lying supine soon after eating has been linked to laryngopharyngeal reflux, and supine sleep has been associated with more frequent sleep paralysis.[1]
The same source reports that lateral position preference rises with age and body mass index, and that one 2025 analysis linked this to a physiological intolerance to the supine position.[1]

Wikipedia's wrinkle article lists habitual sleep position among factors associated with wrinkles, alongside ageing, repeated facial expression, ultraviolet exposure, smoking and other factors, but the article provides no specific study for the sleep-position claim.[2] It also cites a theory that wrinkles arise from imperfect repair of elastic fibres after repeated stretching and compression.[2]

No studies found. No published human trial has tested whether sleeping on the back reduces facial wrinkles or sleep lines. Research on sleep position in general concerns breathing, reflux and similar outcomes.[1]
